idiom_name: NRules: Rule.Define + When()/Then() compiled from expression trees
implementation_notes: NRules is the .NET engine that feels native to C#: rules are classes deriving from Rule, the left-hand side is built by chaining Match/Exists/Not/Query expressions that are compiled as System.Linq.Expressions over typed facts, and the right-hand side by Do(...) actions. The rule repository is compiled once into a factory that creates per-evaluation ISessions, and conditions are real C# expressions, so a renamed property is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise. Compile rules at startup, create a session per unit of work, and route every fact change through the session (Update/Retract) so the engine can maintain matches.
pitfalls: Expression trees accept expressions, not statements: conditions must stay side-effect free and expression-shaped, and imperative C# inside Define() defeats the engine's ability to index and re-evaluate matches.
The session is stateful and not thread-safe: sharing one session across requests accumulates facts and loses isolation - create a session per evaluation and Update/Retract through it.
Rules are only as good as their registration: a rule class the repository never loaded silently never fires, so rule discovery needs a test.

variants.name: Microsoft RulesEngine: JSON workflows with lambda expressions
variants.idiom_name: Microsoft RulesEngine: workflow JSON + expression strings + ExecuteAllRulesAsync
variants.implementation_notes: Microsoft's RulesEngine keeps the rule base entirely outside the code: workflows are JSON documents whose rules carry an Expression string (for example input1.units > 100 AND input1.loyaltyYears > 2) that is parsed into a C# expression against the inputs passed to ExecuteAllRulesAsync. It supports multiple named inputs, scoped params, nested rules and post-execution actions (OutputExpression, EvaluateRule), so the rule store can live in blob storage, configuration or a database and change without a deploy. The price is that nothing type-checks an expression until it runs, and expression text carries the privileges of the process that evaluates it.
pitfalls: A rule expression is a string: a renamed input property or a wrong input1/input2 index fails at run time (or throws), so rule stores need schema validation and a replay test-suite.
The expression language can call injected custom types and methods: whoever can author a rule can usually reach whatever ReSettings exposes - treat rule authoring as a privileged operation.
Rules chained through EvaluateRule actions have no compile-time dependency graph, so a broken chain is only visible in the results of a run.
